description: I'm a solo builder who likes answering hard space questions using real data and developing them into tools anyone can use. For this challenge I took NASA's lunar terrain and orbit data and built a planner that shows where and when to land near the Moon's south pole, and what a crew would need for a successful mission.
summary:
I built Lunar Mission Lab (LML), a web app that helps mission planners in choosing the landing and stay parameters at the Moon's south pole. A planner picks up to eight candidate sites and a landing date. For every hour of the stay, the app shows how much sunlight each site gets, how long the dark spells last, and when Earth is in view for a direct radio link. It then recommends the best site and the best landing date of the year.

The NASA challenge asks for a way to compare landing sites by Sun and Earth visibility over real terrain. My app calculates this from NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL's SPICE ephemeris, tracing the actual skyline around each site.

It matters because at the pole the Sun barely clears the horizon. A ridge a few hundred meters away, or a launch a few days late can leave a lander without power or contact. 

In addition to planning the initial mission parameters, the Expedition view rebuilds the chosen site in 3D from the same NASA elevation data and lights it from the Sun's true position so you can drive a rover across it while gauging battery, sunlight and the Earth link. The Outpost Plan then takes a crew size and stay duration and estimates the solar array and battery each site would need, flagging long darkness, gaps in Earth contact and the impact of a launch delays.
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Mission Lab (LML) helps a mission planner decide where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. You can pick up to eight candidate sites and a landing date, and one screen shows for each site how much of the stay is in sunlight, how long the longest dark spell lasts, when Earth is in view for a direct radio link, and whether the battery survives. The app then recommends the best site and the best landing date of the year. The planner can choose future years, or review the missions from the past.

Behind the scenes, the server traces the real skyline around each site from NASA LOLA elevation data (10 m near the site, 40 m out to 150 km) and takes the positions of the Sun and Earth from JPL's SPICE ephemeris. For every hour of the stay it works out how much of each disc clears the terrain. Nothing is approximated with a flat horizon, and nothing is generated by a language model.

Benefits

At the south pole the Sun sits a degree or two above the horizon, so one ridge can hide it for days. In our example week, three well-known candidate sites get 100%, 84% and 56% sunlight, and a three-day launch slip changes Earth contact at one of them from 100% to 65%. Existing tools can answer these questions one case at a time, for specialists. The LML app puts the comparison on one screen in under a minute.

Intended impact

I wanted site selection to be something a small mission planning team, a student group or a commercial lander company can do with real data. The Outpost Plan takes a crew size and stay duration as inputs to assess the solar array and battery each site would need. In our example, the worst of three sites needs about a hundred times the battery of the best. A single PDF report carries the landing plan and the outpost plan, with every number recalculated on the server.

Tools and Datasets

Tools: Python with SpiceyPy and NumPy for the calculations; TypeScript, Svelte and three.js for the app; Docker and Vercel for hosting.

Data: NASA LOLA terrain, JPL NAIF SPICE kernels, published Artemis candidate sites, NASA's CLPS delivery regions and NASA's landing site records.

What makes it creative

Planners can actually drive the site and target locations with real 10m terrain data. The Expedition view builds the ground from the same NASA heights, lights it from the Sun's true position, and puts you in a rover with live battery, sunlight and Earth-link gauges. Real Landings replays the six Apollo landings and recent missions on their actual dates, so you can see the conditions those crews and landers really had.

Factors considered

Energy (sunlight, darkness and battery size), communications (line of sight to Earth), terrain (slope limits on the rover route), schedule risk (what a launch slip does to the plan), and honesty about limits: every value is an estimate, and the app lists its assumptions under Data and methods.
